title: Bath Salts: Steer Clear
summary: Josh and Chuck examine the designer drug bath salts (synthetic cathinones), tracing its origins from 1920s France and the 2000s web recipe, through the 2010 UK mephedrone craze and its US spread, to the media hysteria over cases like Rudy Eugene in Miami (2012) and Austin Harouff in Florida, where toxicology found no bath salts or flakka. They cover the chemistry (mephedrone, methylone, MDPV), addiction and overdose risks, the federal ban, declining use despite media claims of an epidemic, and the newer drugs flakka (alpha-PVP) and 4-MMC. The episode ends with listener mail about a listener's Simpsons-themed travel and the show's thousandth episode.

segments.title: Opening and live show plugs
segments.summary: Hosts plug upcoming live shows in Seattle and Portland, then introduce the episode on bath salts and the media hysteria around them.

segments.title: Designer drugs and the legal loophole
segments.summary: Bath salts are described as a designer drug, with synthetic cathinone as the active ingredient. Designer drugs are slightly altered chemically to evade bans, creating a cycle hard for enforcement to handle.

segments.title: Mephedrone arrives and bath salts go mainstream
segments.summary: Mephedrone (methedrone, also called meow meow) took off in the UK club scene around 2010 and spread to the US. Bath salts were sold legally at head shops, gas stations and malls under brand names, labeled not for human consumption, at low prices.

segments.title: Effects and how bath salts are used
segments.summary: The hosts describe the typical use (snorting, sometimes injecting or smoking), the packaging, and the reported effects at normal doses. They also read a passage listing severe overdose and chronic-use effects.

segments.title: Media hysteria and the Rudy Eugene case
segments.summary: Media reports attributed violent incidents to bath salts based on a police officer's remark. Rudy Eugene attacked Ronald Poppo in Miami in 2012; he was killed by police, and toxicology found only marijuana. Later reporting still linked the case to bath salts.

segments.title: History of cathinones and khat
segments.summary: Synthetic cathinone was first made in France in the 1920s and resurfaced when its recipe was posted online in the mid-2000s. Haggag, a synthetic version of the plant khat, was popular in Israel. Khat is a leafy plant chewed or brewed in parts of East Africa and the Middle East.

segments.title: Chemistry of bath salts: mephedrone, methylone and MDPV
segments.summary: Bath salts are a mix of mephedrone, methylone and MDPV. Mephedrone forces dopamine release, while MDPV stimulates norepinephrine release and blocks reuptake of norepinephrine and dopamine, which is described as a perfect storm in the brain.

segments.title: Poison control spike and federal ban
segments.summary: UK poison control calls rose sharply in 2010. US states banned bath salts, and the DEA issued an emergency federal ban on mephedrone, methylone and MDPV in 2011.

segments.title: Addiction, overdose risks and declining use
segments.summary: Addiction risk and overdose danger are discussed, with bath salts described as highly addictive and prone to psychotic episodes. Poison control calls peaked in 2011 and halved by 2012, though news outlets called it an epidemic.

segments.title: Flakka and 4-MMC
segments.summary: Newer second-generation drug flakka (alpha-PVP) is discussed, with YouTube videos of users behaving erratically, and the Austin Harouff case in Florida, where no flakka was found in his system. The episode also mentions 4-MMC, known as shrimp.

segments.title: Listener mail and sign-off
segments.summary: A listener named Jerry shares that a Simpsons episode helped him before a job interview, and the hosts plug their social media and email, then sign off.
